conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the bariatric surgery team. I understand you’ve had about a week of epigastric and left upper abdominal pain that feels similar to your prior marginal ulcer pain. Can you tell me what it feels like right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s that sharp pain under my left ribs and it goes through to my mid back. It comes and goes, but last night it got bad again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, black stools, or blood in the stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. No black stools or blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How about reflux, pain with swallowing, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just the stomach pain and my usual nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you taking any NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen? Any smoking or alcohol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No NSAIDs. I don’t smoke or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your G-tube feeds—are you still running them at 60 mL an hour for about 12 hours a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 60 an hour. They’ve been going okay. I’m also eating by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam your belly is soft, and I’m seeing some granulation tissue around the tube site—kind of a small raised area—but no signs of an acute abdomen. Given your history, we’re worried about a recurrent marginal ulcer, even though you’ve been on high-dose Protonix and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I need another scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily during this short stay. First we’ll stabilize symptoms and make sure there’s nothing dangerous like a perforation or obstruction. We’re going to start IV Protonix twice a day and continue sucralfate, and we’ll keep you NPO at first to rest the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: NPO again… I’m worried the pain will get worse if I don’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. The goal is to calm the irritation down. We’ll give IV fluids and a daily vitamin infusion—what we call a banana bag—with thiamine and folate while you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain control? I’m scared it’ll spike overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can start a PCA so you can control small doses for pain. We’ll watch closely for nausea, because opioids can worsen it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get nauseated easily. Can I still have Zofran?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—ondansetron as needed. We’ll also check labs, including nutrition labs, since absorption can be tricky after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They said I’m going for an X-ray. What are you looking for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A plain abdominal X-ray—often called a KUB—to look for free air that could suggest a perforation, and to see the bowel gas pattern for obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your KUB is reassuring: normal bowel gas pattern, no free air, no obstruction. It does show a moderate amount of stool in the colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s constipation causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may contribute to discomfort, but given your history and the way the pain feels, we’re still treating this like possible recurrent ulcer pain. The X-ray mainly helps us rule out emergencies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bloodwork looks stable overall—white count is normal, kidney and liver tests look okay, and lipase is normal. Your hemoglobin is a bit low, and your iron and ferritin are low, which fits iron deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from bleeding from an ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now we don’t see signs of active bleeding—no black stools, no drop in blood counts during this evaluation. After gastric bypass, iron deficiency can happen from absorption issues. We’re going to adjust your iron supplementation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Iron pills upset my stomach. Is there another way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to a liquid iron formulation and dosing it twice a day. We’ll also keep you on your bariatric vitamins—chewable multivitamin, calcium with vitamin D, and weekly B12.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The PCA is helping the pain, but I feel queasy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common side effect. If you’re getting nausea or dry heaving, we may need to back off narcotics and use other strategies. I’m going to ask the chronic pain service to see you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—pain and nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had dry heaves. The pain is a little better, but the nausea was awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the dry heaving, we’re going to stop the narcotics and hold the PCA. We’ll keep the IV Protonix twice daily and sucralfate. The pain team will help adjust your non-opioid regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If you stop the pain meds, won’t the pain come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll still treat pain—just in a way that doesn’t trigger the nausea cycle. One change we expect is increasing your nortriptyline at bedtime, which can help with chronic abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain team mentioned changing my antidepressants. What’s happening with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They recommended increasing nortriptyline to 100 mg at bedtime from 50 mg. They also recommended stopping Effexor. We’ll communicate their recommendations to your psychiatrist, Dr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about stopping meds. Will I feel withdrawal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a fair concern. We’re following the pain service plan and coordinating with your outpatient psychiatrist. If you notice mood changes, anxiety spikes, or other symptoms, tell us right away and we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more result: we checked H. pylori antibody testing, and it’s negative. That makes an H. pylori-driven ulcer less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I keep getting these ulcer symptoms if I’m doing everything right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After Roux-en-Y, the connection between the stomach pouch and small bowel can be prone to irritation in some people even without NSAIDs or smoking. The best-proven steps are exactly what you’re doing: high-dose PPI, sucralfate, and avoiding NSAIDs and tobacco.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m actually hungry now. Can I try something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Let’s start with bariatric Stage 3 diet. If you tolerate it without worsening pain or nausea, we’ll keep advancing slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I kept the Stage 3 down. No vomiting. Mild nausea but way better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll continue Stage 3 for now and keep your tube feeds cycled as you’ve been doing—60 mL per hour for a total of about 760 mL over 12 hours daily—along with your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site has that little bump. Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like granulation tissue—overgrowth of healing tissue—rather than an infection. There’s no fever and your labs don’t suggest infection. If you notice spreading redness, foul drainage, or worsening pain at the site, let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are your symptoms today—pain, nausea, and how you’re doing with the diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is much better. I’m not nauseated now. I’m walking around fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Since you’re stable and tolerating Stage 3, we can plan for discharge later today. You’ll continue pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily and sucralfate 1 gram four times daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I take the sucralfate by mouth or through the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take it by mouth as prescribed. At home you’ve also used it via the G-tube—continue following the instructions you’ve been given for your regimen. The key is four times a day, spaced out from other meds when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nortriptyline—100 at night now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 100 mg at bedtime. We’re also stopping Effexor per the pain service plan, and we’ll make sure your psychiatrist receives the note so your outpatient team can follow you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What diet do I go home on? I don’t want to trigger the pain again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go home on bariatric Stage 3 and advance to Stage 4 and then Stage 5 as tolerated. Continue your cycled tube feeds at 60 mL/hour for 12 hours daily as supplementation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to crush all my pills again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—crush all pills unless you’ve been specifically told not to. It helps with absorption and reduces the risk of irritation after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for that means I need to come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call if you have fever over 101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, pain not relieved by your plan, severe nausea or vomiting, severe bloating, inability to eat or drink, or concerning drainage or redness around the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the iron make me constipated? The X-ray said I had a lot of stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. If you get constipation, you can use a stool softener like Colace twice daily as needed until your bowel pattern is back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved it’s better, but I’m still worried it’ll come back as soon as I’m home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That worry makes sense given your history. The plan at home is the same ulcer-protection strategy that helped here: pantoprazole twice daily, sucralfate four times daily, strict avoidance of NSAIDs, and gradual diet advancement. We’ll have you follow up with Dr. ___ to monitor symptoms and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review your discharge meds: pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily, sucralfate 1 gram four times daily, ondansetron as needed for nausea, nortriptyline 100 mg at bedtime, liquid iron 300 mg twice daily, calcium with vitamin D, weekly B12, and a chewable multivitamin with minerals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. No NSAIDs, crush pills, Stage 3 diet and advance slowly, and keep the tube feeds cycled. I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re stable, walking, and tolerating intake, so we’ll discharge you home now. If anything worsens, don’t wait—call or come in.
